articles.title: Five minutes that matter

body.support:
A **toolbox talk** is a short safety talk. It happens before work starts. It takes about five minutes.

They happen on building sites, in kitchens, in warehouses and on farms.

**A good toolbox talk:**
- is about **one hazard**.
- says why it matters today.
- says what to do.
- asks the group questions.
- ends with everyone signing on.

**How to say it:**
- Stand where everyone can see you.
- Make **eye contact** with the whole group.
- Speak loud and slow.
- Use a calm, serious **tone**.
.
**Listen too.** Ask, “What could go wrong here?” Let people answer. Nod. Say back what they said.

If you are in the group, listen. Ask a question if you’re not sure.
body.core:
A **toolbox talk** is a short safety **briefing** before work starts. It’s usually five to ten minutes, standing up, on site. You’ll find them on building sites, in kitchens, warehouses and farms.

**Purpose and audience.** The purpose is to keep people safe *today*. The audience is the crew: busy, often tired, and keen to start. So keep it short and about one thing.

**Plan it:**
- **Hook:** why this matters today (“Wind’s up to 60 km/h this arvo.”).
- **The hazard:** what could hurt someone, and how.
- **What to do:** two or three clear actions.
- **Questions:** ask the group.
- **Sign-on:** everyone signs to show they were there.

**Deliver it:**
- **Eye contact:** look around the whole group, not at your notes.
- **Body language:** stand still and face people. Don’t fold your arms.
- **Tone:** calm and serious. Not bored, not panicked.
- **Voice:** loud enough for the back row, and slow.
.
**Run the discussion.** Ask **open questions**: “What’s the worst that could happen here?” Then use **active listening**: look at the speaker, nod, and repeat back the main point. Thank people for speaking up, even if they disagree.
body.extend:
A **toolbox talk** is a short, informal safety **briefing** held before work, typically five to ten minutes, on site and standing up. They are common in construction, hospitality, warehousing and agriculture.

**Purpose and audience.** The aim is to focus a crew on one hazard relevant to that day’s work. The audience is time-poor and may have heard many talks before, so relevance and brevity matter more than detail.

**Structure:**
- **hook:** why this hazard matters today.
- **the hazard:** what could happen, to whom, and how.
- **controls:** two or three specific actions.
- **discussion:** open questions to the group.
- **sign-on sheet:** a record that people attended.

**Oral communication:**
- **eye contact** across the whole group shows you mean it, and lets you check people are following.
- **body language:** an open, still stance, facing the group.
- **tone and intonation:** serious and calm; stress key words such as “never” and “before”.
- **pace and volume:** slower and louder than normal talk, especially outdoors.

**Discussion conventions.** Use open questions to draw on the crew’s knowledge: they often know the site’s risks better than the speaker. Practise **active listening**: look at the speaker, don’t interrupt, paraphrase their point, and follow up. A talk where only one person speaks is a lecture, not a toolbox talk.

caseStudies.title: The wall on Swanston Street

body.support:
On **28 March 2013**, a strong wind blew through Melbourne. Gusts reached about **100 km/h**.

On Swanston Street, a brick wall stood next to a building site. A big sign board was fixed to the wall.

The wind pushed on the sign. The wall fell onto the footpath. **Three people walking past were killed.**

Later, the building company, **Grocon**, was fined **$250,000**. So was the sign company.

The sign made the wall less safe in strong wind. A change in the weather can change the danger. That is why crews talk about hazards before work, every day.
body.core:
On **28 March 2013**, strong winds hit Melbourne, with gusts up to about **102 km/h**.

On Swanston Street, in Carlton, an old brick wall stood beside a building site. A large **hoarding** (a sign board) had been fixed to it. The hoarding caught the wind like a sail.

The wall collapsed onto the footpath. **Three people walking past were killed.**

The builder, **Grocon**, was fined **$250,000** in 2014. In 2016, the company that put up the sign was also fined **$250,000**.

Nobody had checked if the wall could hold the sign in strong wind. The weather that day was forecast. It’s the kind of change a daily safety talk is for: today is different, so what could go wrong?
body.extend:
On **28 March 2013**, strong winds struck Melbourne, with gusts recorded up to about **102 km/h**.

On Swanston Street, Carlton, an old masonry wall stood at the edge of a building site. A large **hoarding** had been attached to it, adding a big surface for the wind to push against.

The wall collapsed onto the footpath, **killing three people walking past**.

The builder, **Grocon**, was fined **$250,000** in 2014 over safety failures. The company that installed the hoarding was fined **$250,000** in 2016. A coroner’s inquest in 2018 also found Grocon responsible.

The hazard wasn’t new: the wall had stood for decades. What changed was the hoarding, and then the weather. Toolbox talks exist for exactly this. They are a daily check on what is different today, and a chance for anyone to say “that doesn’t look right”.

model.text:
“Morning, everyone. Quick one today: ladders.
We’ve got gutter work on the north side this week. A fall from a ladder can break bones, or worse.
Three things. Check the feet before you climb. Keep three points of contact. And never stand on the top two rungs.
So, what’s the worst ladder spot on this site?”
[Listen.] “Right, the slope by the shed. Good call, Jas. We’ll use the platform there instead.
Sign on before you head off. Thanks, team.”
why: It opens with why the talk matters this week, not a list of rules.

teacher.overview: Students learn the purpose and structure of a toolbox talk (hook, one hazard, actions, open questions, sign-on), the elements of oral communication (eye contact, body language, tone, intonation, pace) and discussion conventions (open questions, active listening). They plan and run a five-minute toolbox talk for a group. The case study is the 2013 Swanston Street wall collapse, where a hoarding fixed to an old wall, and high winds, led to three deaths.
prep: Book space where students can stand and talk in small groups (outdoors works well).
Arrange cameras or devices for students doing the solo option.
Be aware that the Swanston Street collapse killed three people walking past; handle with care.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — What a toolbox talk is
steps: **Hook (10 min):** show a real toolbox talk video (WorkSafe or industry). What did the speaker do well?

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Plan
steps: **Plan (20 min):** write the talk on one card; practise in pairs.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Run it
steps: **Do it (35 min):** groups of four; each student runs a talk, others join the discussion.
**Reflect (15 min):** peer feedback on eye contact and listening, reflection, sign-off.

teacher.answers:
**Annotation:** 1 hook: why it matters today; 2 one hazard and what could happen; 3 clear, specific actions; 4 open question; 5 active listening and acting on answers; 6 sign-on record.

**Sort:** helps — eye contact around the group; open question; repeating back. Hurts — reading off a phone; “any questions? no? good”; ten hazards.

**Case study:** on 28 March 2013 strong winds (gusts to about 102 km/h) brought down a wall on Swanston Street, Carlton, killing three people walking past; a hoarding attached to the wall caught the wind; Grocon was fined $250,000 (2014) and the sign company $250,000 (2016). The two changes: the hoarding, then the high winds.

realityCheck: **The case study is about real deaths in Melbourne.** Don’t name the people who died. Some students may know of it.
**Speaking to a group is the hard part for many students.** Start in pairs, then fours. The solo video option is a real alternative, not a lesser one.
**Students in trades classes may have done real toolbox talks.** Ask them to model one.
**Works in a real class:** yes. Running it outdoors makes it feel real, and noise forces students to slow down and project.
